Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-20
Time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (IvyGrid Head of Platform), Mark Liu (CTO), Jordan Reyes (DevOps), Priya Patel (Product)

Summary: quick product walkthrough focused on org/project key segmentation, tenant slicing, fair-share rate controls, and graceful backpressure/fallback strategies. Customer wants to understand how Redwood protects production tenants during bursts and how billing/observability tie in.

[00:00] Sofia (Redwood - AE): hey everyone thanks for taking the time, i'm sofia with redwood, with me is ethan our solutions engineer, we'll run through how org and project keys map to quotas, how fair-slicing works and some backpressure patterns. how's that sound?
[00:18] Aisha (IvyGrid): sounds great, thanks sofia. quick context: we run a multi-tenant SaaS for data pipelines, about 120 internal teams, bursty spiky traffic around ETL windows. primary concerns are noisy-neighbor isolation, predictable cost, and ability to route certain VIP tenants to dedicated capacity.
[00:33] Sofia: perfect. ethan, want to take the console and show org/project key mapping?
[00:39] Ethan (Redwood - SE): yeah i'll share my screen. i'm opening the redwood console here — forgive any lag. you can see on the left Projects and Organizations, we typically recommend an org-level key for company-wide quotas and project keys per product team. that lets you do both global budget controls and per-team throttles.
[01:02] Mark (IvyGrid): sorry quick q — what's the difference in behavior between an org key limit and a project key limit during a hard spike? for example if project A hits its limit but org global still has headroom, does project A get rate-limited independently?
[01:14] Ethan: good question. yes, project limits are enforced first — the runtime applies per-key leaky-bucket tokens then an org-level fence. so if project A hits its per-project rate, it will be throttled even if org hasn't hit global. that prevents a noisy team from using org headroom.
[01:31] Aisha: and for VIP tenants we want to route them to Dedicated pools, can we pin a project key to a dedicated pool while the rest remain hosted?
[01:41] Ethan: absolutely. we support sticky routing and key tagging. you can attach routing policies to project keys, so VIP keys get routed to the dedicated capacity or a higher-priority lane with reserved concurrency. if dedicated capacity is saturated, we can fallback to a lower-cost compatible model with an alert.
[01:58] Jordan: interested in fallback — if we fallback to a smaller model during peaks, how do you preserve output quality and avoid silent regressions?
[02:08] Ethan: great point. we recommend defining model variants in the catalog and attaching quality thresholds. redwood optimize will surface expected token cost and a historical quality delta. we also recommend canarying the fallback on a subset of keys and using eval prompt sets to detect regressions, that way you can auto-failback if quality drops below your threshold.
[02:27] Priya (IvyGrid): can you show how that policy looks in the console?
[02:31] Ethan: sure — here's a policy example: route by key -> if usage > 80% for 30s then route to dedicated; if dedicated unavailable then fallback model: gptx-compact (quantized) with holdback 10% sample for quality evaluation. you can tune sample percent and auto-revert rules.
[02:54] Mark: what's the billing implication when a key is pinned to dedicated? do we still get per-token pricing on hosted or is it part of the reserved commit?
[03:04] Sofia: for dedicated it's usually part of the reserved commit. tokens consumed on dedicated are accounted against your capacity commitment, we provide reporting down to project-key level so you can chargeback teams internally. hosted tokens are billed per-usage. we'll include sample invoices in the packet.
[03:20] Aisha: i want to dig into load-shedding and graceful backpressure — during our ETL windows we see 5-10x normal QPS for 3–5 minutes. how does redwood avoid cascading failures?
[03:33] Ethan: there's a few layers. runtime-level: token-bucket per key and per-org, queue depth controls with tail-drop, and adaptive backpressure that pushes a 429 with retry-after hints. control-plane: you can configure over-commit thresholds and burst lanes. also caching: prefix/KV cache for repeated prompts can drastically reduce load.
[03:53] Jordan: retry-after hints — do you recommend exponential backoff or jittered fixed windows? our infra team prefers jitter.
[04:01] Ethan: jittered exponential backoff is best practice. also you can implement client-side throttles using our SDK: it exposes rate-limit headers and a small local leaky-bucket to smooth client retries.
[04:16] [04:16] Sofia: quick clarifying note — some of the documentation names are wrong in the transcript, like K-V cache often shows up as K-V cash in auto transcripts.
[04:24] Aisha: ha noticed that.
[04:27] [04:27] Ethan: for telemetry, you'll get token-level traces, per-key p99/p50, error breakdowns, and per-route histograms in the console. you can also forward traces to your datadog or prometheus.
[04:45] Mark: can we set concurrency caps per key? we need to limit concurrent active requests from any one tenant to protect KV cache and memory.
[04:55] Ethan: yes — concurrency caps are separate from QPS quotas. they enforce max in-flight requests for a key or a project, and we surface queue depth metrics. if concurrency cap is hit, you get an immediate 429 or you can opt for queued waiting with timeout.
[05:10] Aisha: show us an example policy that enforces per-team concurrency plus an org-wide fairness slice.
[05:15] Ethan: pulling policy editor... here's an example JSON policy — (transcription note: policy content paraphrased) set per_project_concurrency: 20, per_org_concurrency: 500, fair_slicing: enabled with weights: projectA:1, projectB:3, VIP:10. that ensures VIP gets more burst headroom while overall org concurrency remains bounded.
[05:40] Jordan: how are weights enforced? is it token-based or request-based?
[05:44] Ethan: request-based but can be token-aware if you attach weight multipliers per route. so long-running requests can be assigned higher weight.
[05:53] [06:05] Aisha: about policing and auditing — we need a full audit trail for compliance. who accessed keys, policy changes, model swaps, etc.
[06:12] Sofia: we provide audit logs (immutable), admin RBAC, SSO with SAML, and KMS integration for key wrapping. for private deployments we can integrate with your HSM. logs are retention-configurable. we'll include the SOC2 section in the packet.
[06:26] Mark: hypothetically, if a rogue script keeps retrying and causing sustained p99 spikes, what automated mitigations can we configure?
[06:36] Ethan: you can configure automated blackholing after N repeated 429s, dynamic throttles that reduce allowed tokens for offending keys, or temporary hold on project keys. plus adaptive sampling to keep critical telemetry while dropping bulk requests.
[06:49] Aisha: do you have an example of the blackhole rule?
[06:52] Ethan: yes, rule: if key returns > 500 errors or > 70% 429s over a 2 minute window then mark key as quarantined for X minutes, notify owner, and optionally auto-unquarantine after a cooldown.
[07:06] Priya: and if we run in Private (VPC) mode, does the control plane still enforce those quotas or do we run a local control plane?
[07:15] Ethan: with Private you get a customer-managed control plane that still uses the same policy engine; you can run it fully air-gapped or connected. enforcement is local to the runtime in your VPC, so quotas and backpressure are enforced within your network boundary.
[07:28] Aisha: okay i want to see a short demo of a spike and how console alerts and metrics look.
[07:33] Ethan: sure i'll simulate a burst using the built-in traffic generator. starting spike now...
[07:40] [07:40] (simulated traffic ramp)
[07:44] Ethan: you can see the p95 jumps, the org-level bucket moves, and a few project keys hit their per-project leaky-buckets. console highlighting: "rate-limited" on three keys, and an alert banner. also showing the live audit entry that notes the policy action.
[08:03] Aisha: perfect — that visual is helpful. how quickly do lambdas or downstream prod systems get the 429s? seconds?
[08:10] Ethan: milliseconds at the runtime level. the decision is synchronous — if the token/bucket won't allow the request we'll return quickly with headers: x-rate-limit-remaining, x-rate-limit-reset, x-request-id.
[08:22] Mark: curious about cold KV cache behavior — if many tenants start different prompts, does cache warm-up cause spikes?
[08:28] Ethan: yes cold cache can cause higher load. that's why we recommend prefix caching for boilerplate prompts and proactive cache warming for known ETL templates. we also support a read-through cache with configurable TTLs.
[08:42] Jordan: about sticky routing — if a key is pinned to dedicated but dedicated is having an outage, can we failover to hosted automatically? what's the latency and risk?
[08:52] Ethan: you can configure automatic fallback with a tolerance window. the request is proxied and the runtime will attempt to route to the next available compatible model. latency impact depends on model size and distance but typically we aim to keep p95 within your SLA by routing to a lower-cost variant in the same region. risk is quality variance — so sample-based evaluation recommended.
[09:12] Aisha: (interruption) sorry — quick interjection from Priya: for product planning we need to know how granular billing is. can we tie spend to project keys and export line-items?
[09:22] Sofia: yes per-project, per-model line items. exportable CSVs broken down by token, model, time window, and note of whether it was served in Dedicated vs Hosted.
[09:33] Mark: a question on throttling semantics — are 429s soft or can we choose to queue requests at the edge?
[09:40] Ethan: both. soft 429 is immediate. alternatively you can enable server-side queuing with max queue depth and per-key timeouts so the runtime attempts to enqueue short-lived spikes. this reduces client retries but increases tail latency.
[09:56] Aisha: are there SDKs to make that easier? our clients are node + python.
[10:01] Sofia: yes, we have official SDKs for node/python/Go. they expose headers, built-in retry helpers with jitter, and local leaky-bucket controls.
[10:11] [10:11] (small cross-talk)
[10:15] Jordan: on the security front — how are keys rotated? automated or manual?
[10:19] Ethan: keys can be rotated via the console or API; for Private deployments you can plug your KMS/HSM for automatic rotation policies. rotation is seamless: existing tokens remain valid for a chosen overlap window. we also support short-lived tokens for ephemeral workloads.
[10:34] Aisha: can you show how RBAC looks when delegating project owners to teams?
[10:39] Ethan: opening RBAC panel — you can create roles: project_admin, read_only, billing_admin. assign roles at org or project scope and enable SSO groups via SAML. changes are audited.
[10:50] Priya: one of our constraints is data residency — some tenants must be kept in eu region. can routing policies pin keys to regions?
[10:58] Ethan: yes routing policies can constrain by region. you can pin keys to european clusters and enforce region-only routing. if geo-unavailable you can fail-closed or fail-open depending on compliance needs.
[11:11] Mark: we run some extremely latency-sensitive flows — could you speak to p99 guarantees on Dedicated?
[11:18] Ethan: Dedicated offers SLA-backed latency targets depending on instance type and configuration. we publish typical p50/p90/p99 profiles per model and hardware in the catalog. for strict p99 you'd reserve capacity and use hot KV caches + shorter sequence lengths.
[11:33] Aisha: can you share a recent benchmark on p99 with a 4k seq on A100-ish hardware?
[11:40] Ethan: i'll attach a link in the follow-up — rough numbers in our catalog show p99 around X ms for that size but i'll run a specific bench for your payload.
[11:49] Sofia: noted, ethan will run a targeted bench using the sample prompt set.
[11:54] [12:04] Ethan: switching gears — talk about observability: every request gets a trace id, token counts, and we compute cost estimates inline. console has per-key cost view so you can enforce budgets.
[12:18] Mark: about budgets — can we set hard stops? e.g., once a project spends $Y for the month, cut them off?
[12:25] Ethan: yes per-project spend caps are supported; you can configure soft alerts and a hard budget that denies further requests once hit. we also support tiered alerts to admins.
[12:36] Aisha: i want to discuss a failure scenario — say a downstream model storage node has slow IO, some requests time out, you start getting 500s. what happens to queued requests?
[12:48] Ethan: the runtime returns 5XX quickly if the model fails; queued requests are retried depending on your retry policy and timeout. we recommend short per-request timeouts and graceful degradation — e.g., fallback to another region or model variant.
[13:02] Priya: do you support preemptible scaling for Dedicated during predictable windows?
[13:09] Ethan: autoscaling policies support scheduled scale-ups and preemptible burst lanes. you can define peak windows and the autoscaler will provision temporary capacity. pricing for burst lanes differs and is shown in the commit.
[13:24] Aisha: are there guardrails to prevent teams from gaming scheduled scale-ups?
[13:29] Ethan: yes policy constraints: scheduled scale-ups require owner approval, and you can set maximum burst multiplier and audit all schedule changes.
[13:38] Mark: how does multitenant KV cache work? is data ever shared across tenants?
[13:45] Ethan: cache is tenant-scoped by default. we do not share KV caches across tenants. there are opaque shared caches for non-sensitive static assets but no PII. for strict compliance you'd use private caches in Dedicated/Private.
[13:59] Jordan: about network egress — any way to limit which external services model code can call?
[14:05] Ethan: for Private you control network egress. for Hosted we provide managed egress with allow-lists and can provide VPC egress options for enterprise accounts.
[14:17] Aisha: i noticed earlier you mentioned prefix caching could reduce token costs — can you explain a common pattern for ETL prompts?
[14:24] Ethan: often ETL prompts share a large boilerplate: instructions, schema, and only swap a small payload. prefix caching stores those static parts so only delta tokens are served to the model, cutting cost and latency.
[14:36] Priya: sounds useful. is prefix caching supported in both Hosted and Private?
[14:40] Ethan: yes, supported across modes. with Private you get more control over cache TTL.
[14:46] Aisha: (pauses) i want to raise procurement questions — if we go Dedicated, what's the minimum commit and lead time?
[14:54] Sofia: min commit varies by region and hardware; typical minimal commercial commitment is 6 months for smaller tiers, 12 for larger, with a lead time of 2-6 weeks depending on capacity. we'll include a specific quote for three-region Dedicated.
[15:10] Mark: are there break clauses if our usage drops?
[15:14] Sofia: contracts have standard ramp and review clauses; we can discuss flexible terms for multi-year commitments.
[15:21] [15:21] Jordan: switching to the technical nitty-gritty — how does continuous batching interact with per-key quotas? during batching, requests from many keys are grouped; could a single key sneak extra tokens in a batch?
[15:35] Ethan: the batching layer is token/account-aware — it enforces quota accounting per-key when forming the batch. we track token usage attributable to each key so you can't exceed quotas by piggybacking on batch composition. there's a small rounding caveat but it's accounted and visible in traces.
[15:55] Aisha: good to know. also curious about cold-starts when model versions change — how do rollouts avoid spikes from cache misses?
[16:03] Ethan: we recommend staged rollouts and cache warmers. rollouts can be canaryed by key and percent. you can also pre-warm weights and KV caches in dedicated pools before traffic flips.
[16:14] Priya: do you integrate with CD systems like Jenkins or GitHub Actions for rollout automation?
[16:19] Ethan: yes APIs and webhooks to integrate with CI/CD and automate rollouts, revert, and policy changes.
[16:28] Aisha: back to quotas — can we set different enforcement modes? e.g., soft throttling (notify, allow) vs hard deny?
[16:36] Ethan: enforcement modes: soft (warn + metrics), hard (deny with 429), queue (enqueue up to timeout), degrade (serve smaller model). you can mix per-route.
[16:48] Mark: let's talk about token accounting accuracy — how do you handle non-deterministic tokenizers or varying token counts across model variants?
[16:57] Ethan: we report tokens based on the actual tokenizer used for the model variant that served the request. for cost alignment we normalize against a reference tokenizer in billing reports. so you'll get both actual tokens and normalized cost tokens.
[17:14] Aisha: (short) will you include a sample billing export?
[17:17] Sofia: yes, included in follow-up.
[17:20] [17:20] Ethan: quick demo of an incident playbook — here's a screenshot (transcribed): "incident: high 5xx rate for model variant x in eu-west-1; remediation: failover traffic to variant y, notify oncall, quarantine offending key if repeat offenders".
[17:38] Mark: who gets alerted from our side? can we map alerts to our pager duty?
[17:43] Ethan: yes you can integrate with PagerDuty/Slack/email and map to your teams; alerting rules are configurable per org/project.
[17:52] Aisha: let's talk final details — for the POC we want a 2-week pilot, dedicated pool for 1 VIP tenant plus hosted for others, and a simple breach-and-fallback policy. can you support that?
[18:03] Sofia: yes that's feasible. we'll propose: 2-week trial with limited dedicated capacity in one region, instrumentation + benching, and a follow-up scoping to finalize the contract.
[18:14] Priya: any blockers on our side? we need to provide sample traffic and an internal contact for SSO and network setup.
[18:21] Aisha: i will own the SLO and sample traffic. jordan will own networking.
[18:26] Sofia: perfect. i'll email the SOC2 and pricing and ethan will run the bench.
[18:32] [18:32] (wrap-up)
[18:34] Sofia: quick recap: next steps: sofia send security + pricing, ethan run bench, ivygrid share traffic. we'll plan poc scoping in two weeks. any last questions?
[18:45] Mark: no, thanks. this was good.
[18:48] Aisha: thanks everyone.
[18:50] Sofia: thanks all, talk soon.
